text: Every named STEP REST API call this app is coded to use -- route template, input, and what it returns -- so the app never hardcodes a STEP URL inline.

Every row is actually called somewhere in the codebase; every STEP call the codebase makes has a row here; each route resolves correctly against the real, live STEP server; and each row's documented return shape still matches what STEP actually returns today, not only that the call fires.
The canonical 66-book Bible ordering (book code + ordinal), the single source every book-order-dependent report/index reads instead of hardcoding it.
Exactly 66 rows, ordinals form an unbroken 0-65 sequence with no duplicates, and every book code matches a real live verse.osisId prefix in both directions.
The live STEP servers connection details (base_url, tagged version, timeout) -- so the app never hardcodes where/how it talks to STEP.
Every key is actually read (stepapi.py); the values genuinely work against the real, currently-running STEP server.
Folder/file patterns to exclude from content-index builds -- so a saturating file (e.g. generated prose) does not swamp search results with noise.
Every pattern actually corresponds to a real, still-relevant reason to exclude; correctly matches content_index own dormant/active state.
Per-pattern size-limit overrides for content-index builds, for files that legitimately need a different cap than the default.
Any row present corresponds to a real, still-needed override; 0 rows is correct when content_index itself is dormant.
Small bookkeeping table about the config store itself -- its version label and which database it describes.

config_version is genuinely read (Cfg.config_version, the live fingerprint mechanism); every key present is actually consumed somewhere -- found live 2026-08-30: the database key is not, a minor orphan.
Strong-number accept/reject/synonym rules for the (now retired) candidate-discovery system.
Consistent with its documented retirement -- all rows correctly inactive, matching retract_candidate_system.py; not a live input to anything.
Every generic secondary SQLite index this app declares for its data tables -- table+column set the builder must create.
Every registered index actually exists live with matching columns; every table it names is real; found+fixed live 2026-08-30: escalation_history was missing its registered index entirely.
Per step+condition, what path (ok/pause/stop/etc) a run takes on that outcome, and what message to show -- so failure routing is data, not a hardcoded if/elif chain.
Every active row names a real active step; every path value is a real member of the path vocabulary; inactive rows correspond to conditions the code genuinely no longer produces.
The canonical controlled-vocabulary registry -- every fixed set of allowed values project-wide, one source of truth instead of scattered hardcoded lists.

Every group is actually enforced against live data, with zero violations across the whole dataset; AND, for a group backing a substantive taxonomy (e.g. hib_kind's six-type plurality-by-specificity scheme), the scheme itself has a documented completeness argument, not only an absence of violations observed so far.

The rulebook for how the escalation system itself must behave (source classification, duplicate suppression, module-blocking, documentation-followup obligations), each rule honestly stating whether it is mechanically enforced or session practice.

Every rule claiming mechanical enforcement is actually enforced by the code it names -- found+fixed live 2026-08-30: module_blocking claimed active/wired but the gate was genuinely commented out since escalation #859.
The field-level enforcement engine behind cfg_escalations policies -- what is required on each escalation action (comment at raise, resolution at approval, etc).
Every rules claimed check genuinely fires -- 5 of 10 rows empirically triggered and confirmed working correctly the same session this was reviewed, not just read from code.

THE schema definition for every data table in the app -- column name/type/constraints/FK/expected-enum, read by build_data_tables() to physically create tables and by Db.write() to validate every write.
Every column here matches the live physical schema exactly, in both directions -- confirmed live 2026-08-30 via find_unregistered_tables_and_columns, now 0 drift after fixing 26 rows.
Composite natural-key definitions for tables whose dedup key is more than one column -- read by table_ddl()/Db.upsert() to know what counts as the same row.

Every registered composite key matches a real live unique index; a table with a genuine composite PK must use THIS table, never repeated is_pk=1 flags -- found+fixed live 2026-08-30 (content_index had exactly this mistake).
The state-machine rules for how an escalations next_action+conditions resolve to its actual state -- config-driven instead of a hardcoded if/elif chain.

Every priority/condition/resulting-status combination genuinely fires correctly for real transactions -- confirmed live 2026-08-30 (the needs_claude_followup fix, tested end-to-end, 6/6 passing both directions).
Documents which status values an entity (escalation, prose_section, word) can hold and what sets each one -- a reference table for _status_for()s substring lookup, not itself the primary mechanism.

Every status genuinely reachable that _status_for() actually resolves to is described here -- found+fixed live 2026-08-30 (extended the re-assigned rows set_by text to also cover the new needs_claude_followup case).
Which writer (a step, or a dispatcher-internal identity) may write which table in which database -- the authorization layer _grant()/may_write() checks before any write.

Every real write in the app goes through a matching grant; a table with no grant at all is unreachable via the sanctioned path; and every grant's scope is one the writer should actually be trusted with, checked against what kind of table it is (rule table vs. data table vs. immutable log), not only that the grant exists and technically permits the write.
The universal registry of every table in the project, config and data alike -- one row per table with its grain and use, read by build_data_tables() and configmaints own what-may-I-touch scan.
Every real live table (in either database) has a row; every rows use text is accurate -- confirmed 0 drift 2026-08-30 via find_unregistered_tables_and_columns after fixing 3 tables.

The top-level categories of project-wide operational behaviour (chat, terminal, sqlite, documentation, llm_output, development, filing) -- each with an authoritative doc and a one-line scope description.

No class boundary is ambiguous -- no rule could plausibly belong to two classes; AND the classes are actually exhaustive of what the project needs regulated, checked by testing whether any real behaviour rule, present or needed, fails to fit cleanly into one of them, not assumed from the fact that none currently does.

The actual behaviour rules within each class -- concrete, individually statable disciplines (e.g. fix the cause not the instance, git commit-and-push together) that govern how work on this project gets done.

Every rule is a real, distinct, non-duplicated discipline, all active; AND every documented incident that produced a corrective lesson -- an escalation, a session-log 'caught myself' entry, a researcher correction -- has a corresponding rule, checked against the actual incident record rather than assumed from the rule table's own completeness-feeling.

Per-step interpretive/methodological guidance the handler follows (e.g. every human mentioned is a presumptive HIB candidate) -- substantive judgement-call rules, distinct from cfg_quality_checks pass/fail tests.

Every active rule is genuinely consulted by its step's real handler code, not just documentation nobody reads, and source_doc traces to a real authoritative instruction; AND the rule set for each step, checked against its governing method document, has no substantive requirement missing outright -- the same derive-independently-first discipline as cfg_quality_check.
Module-scoped settings for the passage subsystem (report paths etc) -- same shape as cfg_setting but dedicated to one module per the has-a-very-good-reason rule.

Every key is actually read by passage-module code, and values correctly reflect where passage.validate's own output really lands today; AND that current behaviour is confirmed as the researcher's actual intended destination/shape, not merely self-consistent with wherever the code happens to write, which would pass even if the current behaviour itself were wrong.
Module-scoped settings for the prose subsystem (chapter names, output/patch paths etc).

Every key genuinely read by prosestore.py, and values match where prose files actually get written; AND that current behaviour is confirmed as the researcher's actual intended destination/shape, not merely self-consistent with wherever the code happens to write, which would pass even if the current behaviour itself were wrong.

Pointers from a named project concept (e.g. verse_primacy) to the prose section that authoritatively defines it -- so a concepts definition lives in exactly one place, never restated as a separate rule.

Every concept_key's chapter/section_hint actually resolves to a real, current prose_section; AND the concept is actually dereferenced at the point of use by the code path that depends on understanding it -- not merely named in a comment, escalation, or migration docstring. Every row should be traceable to at least one real call site that reads it.

Per-step data-quality questions a handler asks of its own output -- distinct from cfg_method_rule's interpretive guidance and cfg_escalation_requirement's field-level gate -- read alongside, and only interpretable against, the actual governing method document for that step (e.g. WA-passage-read-guidance-v1.5, WA-interpretation-questions-v1.4), not as a self-contained list.
Every required checks enforced_by mechanism genuinely exists and runs; every checks test_kind matches how it is actually verified.
Per-report-step presentation settings (title, TOC, output format, naming/archiving scheme) -- how a generated report should look and where it lives.
Every step name is a real active cfg_step; the actual generated report output genuinely matches these settings.
Which tables get a CSV export alongside a given report, and how to join/label them.
Every table_name is a real table or explicitly virtual -- already directly checked this session (find_bad_report_csv_table_references, escalation #1052), confirmed working.
The ordered section structure (heading, TOC label, include/exclude) of a generated report.

Every step is real and active, and the actual generated report's structure genuinely matches this ordering; AND the section order and inclusion set actually gives a sensible, readable report anatomy for its audience -- right sections present in a sensible order, nothing structurally important silently omitted.

Two genuinely different things sharing one table by convention rather than design: (a) standalone project-wide policy with no dedicated table (most of the governance module), and (b) subsystem-scoped operational tuning, some of which has not been reconciled against a subsystem's own dedicated config table where one already exists.
Every key is read via cfg.setting()/required_setting() somewhere live; every key has a real module attribution -- the governance.* slice (46 rows) already confirmed 100% clean 2026-08-30.
The master step registry -- every dispatchable operation in the app, its handler, scope, what it does, and whether it is active -- the backbone run.py reads to resolve a step_id to real code.
Every active steps handler actually resolves to a real, importable function; every step referenced anywhere else (cfg_on_fail, cfg_write_grant, work packages) is a real row here.

The registry of every script/module in the project -- what it is, whether it is config-exempt and why, whether a crash there has been reviewed -- the completeness backbone for is every piece of code accounted for.
Every real .py file doing project work has a row; every rows file_path genuinely exists on disk.
The top-level PS-script-to-work-package registry -- which script runs which package, whether its steps chain under one run_id, and the researcher-facing pause/complete messages.
Every ps_script path is a real file; every name matches a real cfg_step.work_package grouping; chained correctly reflects whether the PS script actually loops its whole sequence.
